newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Cost cutting lifts RJB profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Cost cutting lifts RJB profits.

text.p: Britain's biggest coal producer RJB Mining Plc on Tuesday reported a 9.3 percent rise in 1996 profit, despite a fall in sales as fierce competition continued from natural gas.
But Britain's coal industry was doing better than many had expected, said RJB, which bought most of the surviving coal mines in England when they were privatised in 1992.
"Everybody had forecast that the coal industry would be decimated by now, but in actual fact it is very alive and well," chief executive Richard Budge told Reuters.
Britain's coal market totalled 63 million tonnes last year while many forecasts were for less than 50 million, he said.

Pre-tax profit rose to 189.2 million pounds ($307.7 million) -- which was better than industry analysts had expected. The rise from 173.1 million pounds the year before came as RJB vigorously continued its cost-cutting drive launched after it bought the bulk of British Coal in 1994.

Coal sales fell to 37.6 million tonnes from 41.9 million as the British power industry continued the "dash for gas" -- the switch to natural gas after the European Union repealed a directive banning its use to fuel power stations.
Last year, only 49 percent of Britain's energy was generated by coal compared with about 80 percent in 1990.

The company's core underground mining operations produced 27.7 million tonnes of coal last year, down from 29.9 million in 1995. Production at opencast mines, which make up 20 percent of total output, remained unchanged at 7.2 million tonnes.
RJB still sells a significant part of its production to electricity generators PowerGen Plc and National Power under long-term contracts, but these expire in 1998.
However, Budge said the power generators would realise it was unwise to become overdependent on gas. "Without a mixed portfolio we will be held ransom by gas in the future," he said.
His comments followed Monday's announcement by National Power that it might build a "clean coal" power station in partnership with RJB and Texaco Inc.

Coal demand in the long term would also be underpinned by a wide recognition that it was undesirable for Britain to import large amounts of energy for power generation in the next century, Budge said.
"It (coal) is our only sustainable long-term energy source with decades of coal available at competitive prices, whereas more and more gas in the next century will be coming from Algeria and Russia."
Budge said RJB's sales so far this year had been "satisfactory", but he declined to elaborate.
RJB raised its 1996 dividend by 25 percent to 20.0 pence per share from 16.0 pence. RJB shares advanced five pence to 395-1/2 in late morning trade. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
